newsitem.title: FRANCE: French centre-right supports flexibility on euro.
newsitem.headline: French centre-right supports flexibility on euro.

text.p: A spokesman for France's centre- right, battling for re-election, said on Thursday the coalition believed a European single currency should not be delayed because of failure to strictly meet the criteria for monetary union.

The new flexibilty brought the coalition's position closer to that of the opposition Socialists and marked a departure from statements before the election campaign stressing the need for rigorous adherence to the single currency requirements.
The Socialists say they support monetary union, but oppose a new bout of austerity simply to fulfill a strict interpretion of the Maastricht treaty on European union.
"I would prefer we respect the criteria if possible," said Nicolas Sarkozy, who served as budget minister and government spokesman for ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur.
He is now mentioned as a likely contender for a cabinet post should the right win France's election runoff on Sunday.
But "there is a complete consensus, truly widespread, in the majority...monetary union will not be rejected because we are not exactly at 3.0 percent," Sarkozy told journalists.

The Maastricht treaty calls for public deficits to be cut to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, although it allows for some unspecified margin of overshoot if a country has made steady progress toward the target.
"The treaty...allows an analysis in terms of trend," Sarkozy said. "We have to hold on to this commonsense idea."
Earlier this week, outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe said it was "obvious a second decimal point will be interpreted with intelligence and not using rigorous accounting methods."
"Rather than arguing about 3.1 or 3.2 percent" it was more important that as many countries as possible joined in launching the euro currency, Juppe said.
The government has been seeking to reassure voters ahead of Sunday's final voting round of the two-stage general elections that not much more austerity would be needed to qualify for monetary union.
But the coalition's stand puts it at odds with Germany which has said the 3.0 percent deficit target cannot be waived.
The unpopular Juppe pledged to step down whatever the outcome of the runoff in a bid to salvage the coalition's chances after last Sunday's first round handed a surprise victory to the left.

Sarkozy agreed with Juppe that it was vital to have as many countries as possible in the first wave of monetary union and said postponing the 1999 start could have "major consequences" for closer European union.

Sarkozy, like Juppe and President Jacques Chirac a member of the Gaullist RPR party, added that if one of the single currency's aims was to avoid competitive devaluations, "it would be better to have the southern countries (such as Italy) in the euro rather than to exclude them."

A recent European Union report said Italy would end 1997, the qualifying year for monetary union, with a deficit equal to 3.2 percent of GDP which would disqualify it if Maastricht were interpreted strictly.
Italy has said, however, that it is confident it will hit the 3.0 percent target.
